Hypothesis: Service mix shifted toward slower certificate/scholarship requests
Test: Compare service shares and service-standardised SLA rate
Decision rule / evidence sought: Mix shift contributes to decline; within-service rates also fall
Finding: Supported: mix shift is a measurable contributor, not the only driver

Hypothesis: Two offices experienced a structural capacity/processing shock
Test: Compare office-level SLA rates and Q2 vs Q1 changes
Decision rule / evidence sought: PUN05/PUN06 deteriorate more than peer offices
Finding: Supported in synthetic data: Q2 office shock is concentrated in PUN05/PUN06

Hypothesis: Deadline rushes explain most of the fall
Test: Compare deadline vs non-deadline weeks and exclude deadline weeks
Decision rule / evidence sought: Drop largely disappears outside deadline periods
Finding: Rejected as primary cause: deadline weeks worsen performance but non-deadline decline remains

Hypothesis: Office-code changes created a false reporting decline
Test: Map old/new codes to stable office IDs; compare before/after
Decision rule / evidence sought: Trend materially improves after code harmonisation
Finding: Rejected: harmonisation prevents split-office artefact but does not remove decline

Hypothesis: Duplicate citizen/mobile identities inflated request counts
Test: Deduplicate using citizen_id and request_id; compare unique-citizen view
Decision rule / evidence sought: Headline decline materially changes after deduplication
Finding: Rejected: request-level SLA rate remains directionally similar under citizen-level aggregation

Hypothesis: A district-wide processing slowdown affected all services equally
Test: Compare service and district rates; test interaction
Finding: Rejected: deterioration is heterogeneous by office and service; not uniform
